references.authors: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
references.title: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025.
references.finding: ADA Standards of Care 2025 diagnostic criteria: HbA1c 5.7-6.4% or fasting glucose 100-125 mg/dL defines prediabetes; HbA1c >=6.5% or fasting glucose >=126 mg/dL defines diabetes, with HbA1c unreliable in conditions that alter red-cell turnover.

references.authors: Shah VN, DuBose SN, Li Z, et al.
references.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring Profiles in Healthy Nondiabetic Participants: A Multicenter Prospective Study.
references.finding: In healthy people wearing a blinded Dexcom G6, mean glucose was 98-99 mg/dL (104 over age 60), 96% of time was 70-140 mg/dL, within-person CV was 17%, and glucose was >140 mg/dL for a median 30 minutes a day.

references.authors: Hall H, Perelman D, Breschi A, et al.
references.title: Glucotypes reveal new patterns of glucose dysregulation.
references.finding: Some people classed as normoglycemic by standard tests showed high CGM variability, reaching prediabetic ranges 15% and diabetic ranges 2% of the time; glucose responses to standardized meals varied widely between people.

references.authors: Howard R, Guo J, Hall KD
references.title: Imprecision nutrition? Different simultaneous continuous glucose monitors provide discordant meal rankings for incremental postprandial glucose in subjects without diabetes.
references.finding: Two CGM brands worn at the same time ranked the same person's meals discordantly (Kendall tau 0.43), so meal choices based on one device lost about half the glycemic benefit as judged by the other; CGM-guided precision nutrition may be premature.

references.authors: Zeevi D, Korem T, Zmora N, et al.
references.title: Personalized Nutrition by Prediction of Glycemic Responses.
references.n: 800-person cohort plus 100-person validation and a small RCT
references.finding: Glucose responses to identical meals varied widely between people; an algorithm using microbiome and clinical data predicted responses and a personalized diet lowered post-meal glucose in a small blinded trial.

references.authors: Klonoff DC, Nguyen KT, Xu NY, et al.
references.title: Use of Continuous Glucose Monitors by People Without Diabetes: An Idea Whose Time Has Come?
references.finding: Review arguing that CGM use by people without diabetes (prediabetes, wellness, athletics) is expanding and that CGM 'glucotypes' may come to predict diabetes risk, while noting the evidence base is still developing.

references.authors: Monnier L, Mas E, Ginet C, et al.
references.title: Activation of oxidative stress by acute glucose fluctuations compared with sustained chronic hyperglycemia in patients with type 2 diabetes.
references.finding: Urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha correlated strongly with glucose swings (MAGE r = 0.86) and post-meal glucose, but not with HbA1c, suggesting glucose fluctuations drive oxidative stress more than sustained hyperglycemia.

references.authors: Wentholt IM, Kulik W, Michels RP, et al.
references.title: Glucose fluctuations and activation of oxidative stress in patients with type 1 diabetes.
references.n: 25 type 1 diabetes patients plus healthy controls
references.finding: No relationship was found between CGM glucose variability (MODD, MAGE, CONGA) and urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha in type 1 diabetes, contradicting the type 2 diabetes finding.

references.authors: Pearson TA, Mensah GA, Alexander RW, et al.
references.title: Markers of inflammation and cardiovascular disease: application to clinical and public health practice: A statement for healthcare professionals from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Heart Association.
references.finding: AHA/CDC statement: hs-CRP is the inflammatory marker of choice for optional cardiovascular risk assessment, with <1, 1-3 and >3 mg/L as low, average and high risk; values >10 mg/L should prompt a search for infection or inflammation and repeat testing.

references.authors: Kaptoge S, Di Angelantonio E, Lowe G, et al.
references.title: C-reactive protein concentration and risk of coronary heart disease, stroke, and mortality: an individual participant meta-analysis.
references.finding: CRP was continuously associated with coronary disease, stroke, vascular and non-vascular death and several cancers, but the associations with vascular disease depended considerably on conventional risk factors and other inflammatory markers.

references.authors: Curry SJ, Krist AH, Owens DK, et al.
references.title: Risk Assessment for Cardiovascular Disease With Nontraditional Risk Factors: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.
references.finding: USPSTF found insufficient evidence (I statement) that adding hs-CRP, ankle-brachial index or coronary calcium to traditional risk models improves outcomes in asymptomatic adults.

references.authors: Ridker PM, Danielson E, Fonseca FA, et al.
references.title: Rosuvastatin to prevent vascular events in men and women with elevated C-reactive protein.
references.n: 17,802 adults with LDL <130 mg/dL and hs-CRP >=2 mg/L
references.finding: In JUPITER, rosuvastatin cut major cardiovascular events by 44% (HR 0.56) in people with normal LDL but hs-CRP >=2 mg/L, with more physician-reported diabetes.

references.authors: Sniderman AD, Thanassoulis G, Glavinovic T, et al.
references.title: Apolipoprotein B Particles and Cardiovascular Disease: A Narrative Review.
references.finding: Argues that the number of apoB-containing particles, not their cholesterol content, determines atherogenic risk, so apoB unifies and improves on conventional lipid markers.

references.authors: Mach F, Baigent C, Catapano AL, et al.
references.title: 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias: lipid modification to reduce cardiovascular risk.
references.finding: ESC/EAS 2019 dyslipidaemia guideline: LDL-C remains the primary target; apoB is recommended for risk assessment, especially with high triglycerides, diabetes, obesity or very low LDL-C, with secondary apoB goals of <65, <80 and <100 mg/dL by risk category.

references.authors: Garcia-Casal MN, Pasricha SR, Martinez RX, et al.
references.title: Serum or plasma ferritin concentration as an index of iron deficiency and overload.
references.finding: At a threshold of 30 ug/L, ferritin is reasonably sensitive and very specific for iron deficiency in people presenting for care (low-certainty evidence); evidence that high ferritin detects iron overload is very low certainty, and screening performance in healthy people is unknown.

references.authors: European Association for the Study of the Liver
references.title: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on haemochromatosis.
references.finding: EASL haemochromatosis guideline: in HFE C282Y homozygotes, TSAT >45% with ferritin >200 ug/L (women) or TSAT >50% with ferritin >300 ug/L (men, postmenopausal women) suffices for diagnosis; phlebotomy targets ferritin <50 ug/L in induction and <100 ug/L in maintenance.

references.authors: Kowdley KV, Brown KE, Ahn J, et al.
references.title: ACG Clinical Guideline: Hereditary Hemochromatosis.
references.finding: ACG hemochromatosis guideline: ferritin <1,000 ng/mL at diagnosis identifies low risk of advanced fibrosis; elevated ferritin is more often due to fatty liver or alcohol than to hemochromatosis in people who are not C282Y homozygotes or C282Y/H63D compound heterozygotes.

references.authors: Allen KJ, Gurrin LC, Constantine CC, et al.
references.title: Iron-overload-related disease in HFE hereditary hemochromatosis.
references.finding: Documented iron-overload-related disease developed in 28.4% of male but only 1.2% of female C282Y homozygotes; only one non-homozygote (a compound heterozygote) had such disease.

references.authors: Pilling LC, Tamosauskaite J, Jones G, et al.
references.title: Common conditions associated with hereditary haemochromatosis genetic variants: cohort study in UK Biobank.
references.finding: C282Y homozygosity was associated with liver disease (OR 4.30), arthritis, diabetes (OR 1.53) and more incident morbidity in both men (15.7% vs 5.0%) and women (10.1% vs 3.4%), supporting re-examination of early case-finding.

references.authors: Whitlock EP, Garlitz BA, Harris EL, et al.
references.title: Screening for hereditary hemochromatosis: a systematic review for the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force.
references.finding: USPSTF systematic review: up to 38-50% of C282Y homozygotes may develop iron overload and 10-33% hemochromatosis-related morbidity, but evidence was insufficient to estimate the benefit of population genetic screening.

references.authors: Walsh A, Dixon JL, Ramm GA, et al.
references.title: The clinical relevance of compound heterozygosity for the C282Y and H63D substitutions in hemochromatosis.
references.n: 249 C282Y/H63D compound heterozygotes and 483 C282Y homozygotes
references.finding: C282Y/H63D compound heterozygotes often had raised iron indices but did not develop progressive disease without cofactors such as fatty liver, diabetes or excess alcohol.

references.authors: Lee DH, Blomhoff R, Jacobs DR Jr
references.title: Is serum gamma glutamyltransferase a marker of oxidative stress?
references.finding: Proposes that serum GGT within its normal range is an early marker of oxidative stress: it is inversely related to antioxidant vitamins and predicts F2-isoprostanes and CRP measured 5-15 years later in a dose-response manner.

references.authors: Lim JS, Yang JH, Chun BY, et al.
references.title: Is serum gamma-glutamyltransferase inversely associated with serum antioxidants as a marker of oxidative stress?
references.finding: Across all deciles of serum GGT, higher GGT was associated with lower serum carotenoids and vitamin C (not vitamin E), independent of alcohol, smoking and BMI.

references.authors: Kunutsor SK, Apekey TA, Seddoh D, et al.
references.title: Liver enzymes and risk of all-cause mortality in general populations: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Top versus bottom third of GGT was associated with 60% higher all-cause mortality (RR 1.60), roughly linear at 7% per 5 U/L.

references.authors: Nano J, Muka T, Ligthart S, et al.
references.title: Gamma-glutamyltransferase levels, prediabetes and type 2 diabetes: a Mendelian randomization study.
references.finding: Observationally GGT predicted prediabetes and diabetes, but genetically raised GGT did not (causal RR 0.96), suggesting confounding or reverse causation rather than a causal role.

references.authors: Sautin YY, Johnson RJ
references.title: Uric acid: the oxidant-antioxidant paradox.
references.finding: Uric acid is the main plasma antioxidant yet predicts obesity, hypertension and cardiovascular disease; the authors argue its intracellular pro-oxidant actions contribute to disease.

references.authors: Li X, Meng X, Timofeeva M, et al.
references.title: Serum uric acid levels and multiple health outcomes: umbrella review of evidence from observational studies, randomised controlled trials, and Mendelian randomisation studies.
references.finding: Despite hundreds of meta-analyses and Mendelian randomization studies, convincing evidence of a causal role of serum uric acid exists only for gout and kidney stones.

references.authors: Badve SV, Pascoe EM, Tiku A, et al.
references.title: Effects of Allopurinol on the Progression of Chronic Kidney Disease.
references.finding: CKD-FIX: allopurinol lowered urate but did not slow eGFR decline compared with placebo.

references.authors: Doria A, Galecki AT, Spino C, et al.
references.title: Serum Urate Lowering with Allopurinol and Kidney Function in Type 1 Diabetes.
references.n: 530 adults with type 1 diabetes and early kidney disease
references.finding: PERL: allopurinol lowered serum urate but had no clinically meaningful benefit on kidney function.

references.authors: Mackenzie IS, Hawkey CJ, Ford I, et al.
references.title: Allopurinol versus usual care in UK patients with ischaemic heart disease (ALL-HEART): a multicentre, prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial.
references.finding: ALL-HEART: allopurinol did not reduce MI, stroke or cardiovascular death (HR 1.04) versus usual care over 4.8 years.

references.authors: Homocysteine Studies Collaboration
references.title: Homocysteine and risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke: a meta-analysis.
references.finding: A 25% lower homocysteine (about 3 umol/L) was associated with 11% lower ischaemic heart disease and 19% lower stroke risk; homocysteine is at most a modest independent predictor in healthy people.

references.authors: Lonn E, Yusuf S, Arnold MJ, et al.
references.title: Homocysteine lowering with folic acid and B vitamins in vascular disease.
references.n: 5,522 adults with vascular disease or diabetes
references.finding: HOPE-2: folic acid, B6 and B12 lowered homocysteine but did not reduce major cardiovascular events (RR 0.95); stroke was reduced (RR 0.75) and unstable-angina admissions rose.

references.authors: Bønaa KH, Njølstad I, Ueland PM, et al.
references.title: Homocysteine lowering and cardiovascular events after acute myocardial infarction.
references.finding: NORVIT: B vitamins cut homocysteine 27% but did not reduce recurrent cardiovascular events, with a trend toward harm for the combined folic acid-B12-B6 arm (RR 1.22).

references.authors: Martí-Carvajal AJ, Solà I, Lathyris D, et al.
references.title: Homocysteine-lowering interventions for preventing cardiovascular events.
references.finding: Cochrane: homocysteine-lowering B vitamins do not prevent myocardial infarction or death; there may be a small reduction in stroke.

references.authors: Huo Y, Li J, Qin X, et al.
references.title: Efficacy of folic acid therapy in primary prevention of stroke among adults with hypertension in China: the CSPPT randomized clinical trial.
references.finding: CSPPT: adding 0.8 mg folic acid to enalapril reduced first stroke (HR 0.79) in a population without folic acid fortification.

references.authors: Harris WS, Von Schacky C
references.title: The Omega-3 Index: a new risk factor for death from coronary heart disease?
references.finding: Proposes red-cell EPA+DHA (the Omega-3 Index) as a coronary risk factor: >=8% associated with the most and <=4% with the least cardioprotection.

references.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.
references.title: Marine n-3 Fatty Acids and Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer.
references.finding: VITAL: 1 g/day marine omega-3 did not reduce major cardiovascular events or cancer (HR 0.92 and 1.03); myocardial infarction was lower (HR 0.72) as a secondary outcome.

references.authors: Bhatt DL, Steg PG, Miller M, et al.
references.title: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction with Icosapent Ethyl for Hypertriglyceridemia.
references.finding: REDUCE-IT: 4 g/day icosapent ethyl (purified EPA) lowered ischaemic events and cardiovascular death (HR 0.80) versus mineral-oil placebo, with more atrial fibrillation.

references.authors: Nissen SE, Lincoff AM, Wolski K, et al.
references.title: Association Between Achieved ω-3 Fatty Acid Levels and Major Adverse Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients With High Cardiovascular Risk: A Secondary Analysis of the STRENGTH Trial.
references.n: 10,382 STRENGTH participants with fatty acid levels
references.finding: In STRENGTH, the highest achieved plasma EPA or DHA levels on omega-3 carboxylic acids were not associated with fewer cardiovascular events (HR 0.98 and 1.02) versus corn oil.

references.authors: Demay MB, Pittas AG, Bikle DD, et al.
references.title: Vitamin D for the Prevention of Disease: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline.
references.finding: Endocrine Society 2024: suggests empiric vitamin D for children, adults over 75, pregnancy and high-risk prediabetes, and suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing in the absence of established indications.

references.authors: Ross AC, Manson JE, Abrams SA, et al.
references.title: The 2011 report on dietary reference intakes for calcium and vitamin D from the Institute of Medicine: what clinicians need to know.
references.finding: IOM 2011: a serum 25(OH)D of 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) meets the needs of 97.5% of people; higher levels were not consistently linked to more benefit, and deficiency prevalence had been overestimated.

references.authors: Holick MF, Binkley NC, Bischoff-Ferrari HA, et al.
references.title: Evaluation, treatment, and prevention of vitamin D deficiency: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline.
references.finding: Endocrine Society 2011 guideline recommended 25(OH)D testing in people at risk of deficiency (defining deficiency as <20 ng/mL and insufficiency as 21-29 ng/mL) but not screening of people not at risk.

references.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.
references.title: Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease.
references.finding: VITAL: 2,000 IU/day vitamin D3 did not reduce invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events.

references.authors: Krist AH, Davidson KW, Mangione CM, et al.
references.title: Screening for Vitamin D Deficiency in Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.
references.finding: USPSTF found insufficient evidence (I statement) to recommend for or against screening asymptomatic adults for vitamin D deficiency and noted no consensus on the level that defines deficiency.

references.authors: Devalia V, Hamilton MS, Molloy AM
references.title: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of cobalamin and folate disorders.
references.finding: British Society for Haematology: no gold-standard test for cobalamin deficiency; serum B12 is first-line, methylmalonic acid is a more specific second-line test than homocysteine, and fixed cut-offs are not possible.

references.authors: Stabler SP
references.title: Clinical practice. Vitamin B12 deficiency.
references.finding: NEJM clinical review of vitamin B12 deficiency covering causes (including metformin and acid suppression), the limits of serum B12 and the use of methylmalonic acid and homocysteine to confirm deficiency.

references.authors: Hannibal L, Lysne V, Bjørke-Monsen AL, et al.
references.title: Biomarkers and Algorithms for the Diagnosis of Vitamin B12 Deficiency.
references.finding: Serum B12 alone has limited diagnostic value; holotranscobalamin plus methylmalonic acid (>271 nmol/L suggesting deficiency in one algorithm) improve classification.

references.authors: Combs GF Jr
references.title: Biomarkers of selenium status.
references.finding: Plasma selenoproteins (GPX3, selenoprotein P) reach maximal expression at plasma selenium around 50-70 ng/mL; above that plasma selenium mainly reflects non-specific selenomethionine, and supplementation showed no cancer benefit in people above ~120 ng/mL.

references.authors: King JC, Brown KH, Gibson RS, et al.
references.title: Biomarkers of Nutrition for Development (BOND)-Zinc Review.
references.finding: Plasma zinc is the only recommended zinc biomarker, but it responds weakly to intake and is shifted by recent meals, time of day, inflammation, drugs and hormones; oxidative-stress markers are not recommended for assessing zinc status.

references.authors: Kwo PY, Cohen SM, Lim JK
references.title: ACG Clinical Guideline: Evaluation of Abnormal Liver Chemistries.
references.finding: ACG guideline on abnormal liver chemistries: healthy upper limits of ALT are lower than many laboratory ranges, and abnormal values should prompt evaluation for fatty liver, alcohol, viral hepatitis, hemochromatosis and drugs.

references.authors: Prati D, Taioli E, Zanella A, et al.
references.title: Updated definitions of healthy ranges for serum alanine aminotransferase levels.
references.finding: Updated healthy ALT upper limits (30 U/L men, 19 U/L women) were lower than conventional limits; ALT tracked BMI and lipid and glucose abnormalities.

references.authors: Kadiiska MB, Gladen BC, Baird DD, et al.
references.title: Biomarkers of oxidative stress study II: are oxidation products of lipids, proteins, and DNA markers of CCl4 poisoning?
references.finding: In the multi-laboratory BOSS validation study in CCl4-poisoned rats, plasma and urinary F2-isoprostanes and MDA (by GC-MS) and urinary 8-OHdG were the best-performing oxidative-stress biomarkers.

references.authors: Milne GL, Musiek ES, Morrow JD
references.title: F2-isoprostanes as markers of oxidative stress in vivo: an overview.
references.finding: F2-isoprostanes, formed by free-radical peroxidation of arachidonic acid, are accurate in vivo measures of lipid peroxidation when quantified by mass spectrometry.

references.authors: Collins AR, Cadet J, Möller L, et al.
references.title: Are we sure we know how to measure 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine in DNA from human cells?
references.finding: ESCODD found published background levels of 8-oxoguanine in human DNA varied hugely because of oxidation artefacts during sample work-up; chromatographic methods were unreliable at low levels.

references.authors: Barregard L, Møller P, Henriksen T, et al.
references.title: Human and methodological sources of variability in the measurement of urinary 8-oxo-7,8-dihydro-2'-deoxyguanosine.
references.finding: ELISA results for urinary 8-oxodG varied more than chromatographic assays and could not determine absolute levels; within-person day-to-day CV was about 17-20%.

references.authors: Frijhoff J, Winyard PG, Zarkovic N, et al.
references.title: Clinical Relevance of Biomarkers of Oxidative Stress.
references.finding: Oxidative-stress biomarkers are often measured with non-specific methods, while specific methods are too laborious for routine use; none is yet validated as a clinical diagnostic.

references.authors: Sies H
references.title: Total antioxidant capacity: appraisal of a concept.
references.finding: Plasma 'total antioxidant capacity' is a misnomer because major antioxidant defense is enzymatic; it mainly reflects urate, ascorbate and tocopherol, which should be measured directly instead.

references.authors: Pompella A, Sies H, Wacker R, et al.
references.title: The use of total antioxidant capacity as surrogate marker for food quality and its effect on health is to be discouraged.
references.finding: Using total antioxidant capacity assays (ORAC, FRAP, TEAC) as markers of food quality or health effect should be discouraged; a higher plasma TAC is often wrongly read as beneficial.

references.authors: Mather KA, Jorm AF, Parslow RA, et al.
references.title: Is telomere length a biomarker of aging? A review.
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.finding: Evidence that leukocyte telomere length is a biomarker of human ageing is equivocal; longitudinal studies are needed.

references.authors: Martin-Ruiz CM, Baird D, Roger L, et al.
references.title: Reproducibility of telomere length assessment: an international collaborative study.
references.finding: Inter-laboratory CVs were about 10% for Southern blot and over 20% for qPCR telomere measurement, which precludes shared reference ranges between laboratories.

references.authors: Haycock PC, Burgess S, Nounu A, et al.
references.title: Association Between Telomere Length and Risk of Cancer and Non-Neoplastic Diseases: A Mendelian Randomization Study.
references.n: Mendelian randomization across 35 cancers and 48 non-neoplastic diseases
references.finding: Genetically longer telomeres were associated with higher risk of several cancers and lower risk of some non-neoplastic diseases such as coronary heart disease, so longer is not simply better.

references.authors: World Health Organization
references.title: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, sixth edition
references.finding: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, 6th edition (2021): standardized methods and fifth-centile values from fertile men (volume 1.4 mL, concentration 16 million/mL, total 39 million, total motility 42%, progressive 30%, vitality 54%, normal forms 4%), plus extended tests such as sperm DNA fragmentation and seminal oxidative stress.

references.authors: Campbell MJ, Lotti F, Baldi E, et al.
references.title: Distribution of semen examination results 2020 - A follow up of data collated for the WHO semen analysis manual 2010.
references.finding: Updated fertile-men fifth centiles were 16 million/mL, 30% progressive motility (42% total) and 4% normal forms; these do not draw a sharp line between fertile and subfertile men.

references.authors: Guzick DS, Overstreet JW, Factor-Litvak P, et al.
references.title: Sperm morphology, motility, and concentration in fertile and infertile men.
references.finding: Subfertile thresholds were <13.5 million/mL, <32% motility and <9% normal forms and fertile thresholds >48 million/mL, >63% and >12%, but fertile and infertile men overlapped extensively; no single measure was diagnostic.

references.authors: Boitrelle F, Shah R, Saleh R, et al.
references.title: The Sixth Edition of the WHO Manual for Human Semen Analysis: A Critical Review and SWOT Analysis.
references.finding: The 6th WHO manual strengthened methods and described SDF and oxidative-stress tests but replaced reference limits with 'decision limits' that it never actually provides.

references.authors: Schlegel PN, Sigman M, Collura B, et al.
references.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Infertility in Men: AUA/ASRM Guideline Part I.
references.finding: AUA/ASRM male infertility guideline part I: evaluation with at least two semen analyses, hormonal testing (FSH, testosterone) in men with abnormal semen parameters or symptoms, and recognition that male infertility marks higher risk of other health problems; routine DNA fragmentation and ROS testing are not recommended in the initial evaluation.

references.authors: Brannigan RE, Hermanson L, Kaczmarek J, et al.
references.title: Updates to Male Infertility: AUA/ASRM Guideline (2024).
references.finding: 2024 AUA/ASRM amendment updated thresholds for Y-microdeletion testing, MRI indications and guidance on testicular sperm in non-azoospermic men.

references.authors: Minhas S, Bettocchi C, Boeri L, et al.
references.title: European Association of Urology Guidelines on Male Sexual and Reproductive Health: 2021 Update on Male Infertility.
references.finding: EAU 2021: infertile men should be screened for modifiable risks such as hypogonadism; sperm DNA fragmentation testing can identify infertile men and inform ART outcomes; antioxidants and other empirical treatments lack high-quality evidence.

references.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
references.title: The clinical utility of sperm DNA integrity testing: a guideline.
references.finding: ASRM Practice Committee: sperm DNA integrity tests do not reliably predict treatment outcomes and cannot be recommended routinely.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Majzoub A, Baskaran S, et al.
references.title: Sperm DNA Fragmentation: A New Guideline for Clinicians.
references.finding: Expert review proposing clinical indications for SDF testing (varicocele, unexplained infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss, failed ART, lifestyle risk) while acknowledging professional societies do not recommend routine testing.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Farkouh A, Saleh R, et al.
references.title: Controversy and Consensus on Indications for Sperm DNA Fragmentation Testing in Male Infertility: A Global Survey, Current Guidelines, and Expert Recommendations.
references.finding: Global survey: ~75% of andrology experts test SDF in unexplained infertility and 39% routinely in recurrent pregnancy loss, despite very few society recommendations; practice is highly heterogeneous.

references.authors: Esteves SC, Zini A, Coward RM, et al.
references.title: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing: Summary evidence and clinical practice recommendations.
references.finding: Expert group formulated 41 recommendations on SDF testing in varicocele, unexplained infertility, recurrent loss, IUI and IVF/ICSI, noting supporting evidence is moderate to low quality.

references.authors: Collins JA, Barnhart KT, Schlegel PN
references.title: Do sperm DNA integrity tests predict pregnancy with in vitro fertilization?
references.finding: Sperm DNA integrity tests had a small association with IVF/ICSI pregnancy (DOR 1.44) but likelihood ratios were not predictive, too weak to justify routine use.

references.authors: Cissen M, Wely MV, Scholten I, et al.
references.title: Measuring Sperm DNA Fragmentation and Clinical Outcomes of Medically Assisted Reproduction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Current SDF tests have limited capacity to predict pregnancy after IVF, ICSI or IUI and should not be used routinely to predict outcome or choose treatment.

references.authors: Robinson L, Gallos ID, Conner SJ, et al.
references.title: The effect of sperm DNA fragmentation on miscarriage rates: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: High sperm DNA damage was associated with doubled miscarriage risk (RR 2.16), strongest with TUNEL (RR 3.94).

references.authors: McQueen DB, Zhang J, Robins JC
references.title: Sperm DNA fragmentation and recurrent pregnancy loss: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.n: 579 male partners of women with recurrent loss and 434 controls
references.finding: Male partners of women with recurrent pregnancy loss had about 12 percentage points higher SDF, with substantial heterogeneity and no prospective outcome data.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Panner Selvam MK, Arafa M, et al.
references.title: Multi-center evaluation of oxidation-reduction potential by the MiOXSYS in males with abnormal semen.
references.finding: Seminal ORP (MiOXSYS) correlated negatively with semen parameters; a cut-off of 1.34 mV/10^6 sperm/mL flagged abnormal semen with 98% sensitivity but 41% specificity.

references.authors: Agarwal A, Parekh N, Panner Selvam MK, et al.
references.title: Male Oxidative Stress Infertility (MOSI): Proposed Terminology and Clinical Practice Guidelines for Management of Idiopathic Male Infertility.
references.finding: Proposes 'Male Oxidative Stress Infertility' (MOSI) as a diagnosis for men with abnormal semen and oxidative stress, using ORP to target antioxidant therapy.

references.authors: Homa ST, Vassiliou AM, Stone J, et al.
references.title: A Comparison Between Two Assays for Measuring Seminal Oxidative Stress and their Relationship with Sperm DNA Fragmentation and Semen Parameters.
references.n: Semen samples from men attending an andrology service
references.finding: Chemiluminescent ROS and MiOXSYS ORP captured different aspects of oxidative stress; leukocyte-rich samples had high ROS but not high ORP or DFI, so neither assay suffices alone.

references.authors: Castleton PE, Deluao JC, Sharkey DJ, et al.
references.title: Measuring Reactive Oxygen Species in Semen for Male Preconception Care: A Scientist Perspective.
references.finding: Clinically marketed semen ROS tests (MiOXSYS, luminol chemiluminescence, OxiSperm) have inconsistent decision limits and no trials showing benefit on fertilization, pregnancy or live birth.

references.authors: Panner Selvam MK, Baskaran S, O'Connell S, et al.
references.title: Association between Seminal Oxidation-Reduction Potential and Sperm DNA Fragmentation-A Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Seminal ORP correlated weakly with SDF (pooled r = 0.24).

references.authors: Joao F, Duval C, Bélanger MC, et al.
references.title: Reassessing the interpretation of oxidation-reduction potential in male infertility.
references.n: 134 men with normal and 574 with abnormal semen
references.finding: Differences in the sORP index between groups were driven mainly by sperm concentration, the index's denominator, rather than by oxidation itself.

references.authors: Henkel R, Morris A, Vogiatzi P, et al.
references.title: Predictive value of seminal oxidation-reduction potential analysis for reproductive outcomes of ICSI.
references.n: Fresh ICSI cycles at one centre
references.finding: Seminal ORP predicted fertilization, blastocyst development, clinical pregnancy and live birth after ICSI about as well as SDF (live birth AUC 0.73).

references.authors: Tan Y, Yuan Y, Yang X, et al.
references.title: Diagnostic value of oxidation-reduction potential for male infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: ORP had pooled sensitivity 0.81 and specificity 0.66 (AUC 0.80) for distinguishing infertile from fertile men.

references.authors: Lundin K, Bentzen JG, Bozdag G, et al.
references.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine†.
references.finding: ESHRE add-ons recommendations: insufficient evidence that SDF tests predict pregnancy or guide treatment, so sperm DNA damage testing is not recommended for routine use; reported ORP-SDF correlations are weak or absent; antioxidant therapy is not recommended in ART.

references.authors: Steiner AZ, Pritchard D, Stanczyk FZ, et al.
references.title: Association Between Biomarkers of Ovarian Reserve and Infertility Among Older Women of Reproductive Age.
references.n: 750 women aged 30-44 trying to conceive for <=3 months
references.finding: Low AMH (<0.7 ng/mL) or high FSH (>10 mIU/mL) was not associated with lower chance of natural conception by 6 or 12 cycles (65% vs 62% at 6 cycles for low vs normal AMH).

references.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
references.title: Testing and interpreting measures of ovarian reserve: a committee opinion.
references.finding: ASRM: ovarian reserve markers (AMH, AFC, FSH) predict egg yield after stimulation but are poor predictors of reproductive potential independent of age.

references.authors: Broer SL, van Disseldorp J, Broeze KA, et al.
references.title: Added value of ovarian reserve testing on patient characteristics in the prediction of ovarian response and ongoing pregnancy: an individual patient data approach.
references.finding: AMH or AFC predicted poor ovarian response (AUC 0.78 and 0.76) but added nothing to age in predicting ongoing pregnancy after IVF.

references.authors: Iliodromiti S, Kelsey TW, Wu O, et al.
references.title: The predictive accuracy of anti-Müllerian hormone for live birth after assisted conception: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the literature.
references.finding: AMH had a weak association with live birth after assisted conception (DOR 2.4) independent of age, but poor predictive accuracy.

references.authors: Depmann M, Broer SL, Eijkemans MJC, et al.
references.title: Anti-Müllerian hormone does not predict time to pregnancy: results of a prospective cohort study.
references.finding: After age adjustment, AMH, AFC and basal FSH did not predict time to ongoing pregnancy.

references.authors: Nelson SM, Shaw M, Ewing BJ, et al.
references.title: Antimüllerian hormone levels are associated with time to pregnancy in a cohort study of 3,150 women.
references.finding: Low AMH (<1 ng/mL) was independently associated with a modest reduction in per-cycle chance of conception (11.2% vs 14.3% at cycle four).

references.authors: Copp T, Thompson R, Hammarberg K, et al.
references.title: Attitudes, knowledge and practice regarding the anti-müllerian hormone test among general practitioners and reproductive specialists: A cross-sectional study.
references.finding: Many clinicians ordered AMH tests for reproductive planning or reassurance, uses not supported by evidence, and half lacked confidence interpreting results; direct-to-consumer testing is growing.

references.authors: Broekmans FJ, Kwee J, Hendriks DJ, et al.
references.title: A systematic review of tests predicting ovarian reserve and IVF outcome.
references.finding: Systematic review: ovarian reserve tests predict poor response only modestly and pregnancy very poorly; their use for IVF outcome prediction cannot be supported.

references.authors: Pipari A, Guillen A, Cruz M, et al.
references.title: Serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels are not associated with aneuploidy rates in human blastocysts.
references.finding: AMH was not associated with blastocyst aneuploidy rates; higher AMH gave more embryos, not better ones.

references.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Ovarian Stimulation (Bosch E, Broer S, et al.)
references.title: ESHRE guideline: ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI(†).
references.finding: ESHRE ovarian stimulation guideline: strong recommendation to use AFC or AMH, rather than other ovarian reserve tests, to predict high and poor response.

references.authors: Gasper AV, Al-Janobi A, Smith JA, et al.
references.title: Glutathione S-transferase M1 polymorphism and metabolism of sulforaphane from standard and high-glucosinolate broccoli.
references.finding: GSTM1-null subjects had higher plasma sulforaphane and excreted more of it than GSTM1-positive subjects after broccoli; genotype altered sulforaphane metabolism.

references.authors: London SJ, Yuan JM, Chung FL, et al.
references.title: Isothiocyanates, glutathione S-transferase M1 and T1 polymorphisms, and lung-cancer risk: a prospective study of men in Shanghai, China.
references.n: 232 lung cancer cases and 710 controls nested in 18,244 men
references.finding: Detectable urinary isothiocyanates were linked to lower lung cancer risk (RR 0.65), most strongly in GSTM1-null (0.36) and GSTM1/GSTT1 double-null men (0.28).

references.authors: Steck SE, Gammon MD, Hebert JR, et al.
references.title: GSTM1, GSTT1, GSTP1, and GSTA1 polymorphisms and urinary isothiocyanate metabolites following broccoli consumption in humans.
references.finding: GST genotypes did not substantially change isothiocyanate excretion; GSTM1-null subjects were more often high excreters (62% vs 39%).

references.authors: Wu W, Lu J, Tang Q, et al.
references.title: GSTM1 and GSTT1 null polymorphisms and male infertility risk: an updated meta-analysis encompassing 6934 subjects.
references.finding: GSTM1 null genotype was associated with a significantly higher risk of male infertility in Asian and Caucasian groups; GSTT1 findings were inconsistent.

references.authors: Méar L, Herr M, Fauconnier A, et al.
references.title: Polymorphisms and endometriosis: a systematic review and meta-analyses.
references.finding: Among many studied polymorphisms, GSTT1 null was among the few robustly associated with endometriosis, while GSTM1 null was among candidates needing confirmation in well-defined cohorts.

references.authors: Bag A, Bag N
references.title: Target sequence polymorphism of human manganese superoxide dismutase gene and its association with cancer risk: a review.
references.finding: The SOD2 (MnSOD) Val16Ala polymorphism showed no overall association with breast or total cancer risk (OR 0.98-1.02).

references.authors: Ji G, Gu A, Wang Y, et al.
references.title: Genetic variants in antioxidant genes are associated with sperm DNA damage and risk of male infertility in a Chinese population.
references.finding: SOD2 Val16Ala and PON1 Arg192Glu variants were associated with male infertility and higher sperm DNA fragmentation and 8-OHdG in a Chinese population.

references.authors: Hickey SE, Curry CJ, Toriello HV
references.title: ACMG Practice Guideline: lack of evidence for MTHFR polymorphism testing.
references.finding: ACMG: MTHFR polymorphism testing has minimal clinical utility and should not be part of routine thrombophilia evaluation; meta-analyses disproved links with venous thrombosis and coronary disease.

references.authors: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists' Committee on Practice Bulletins–Obstetrics
references.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 197: Inherited Thrombophilias in Pregnancy.
references.finding: ACOG Practice Bulletin 197 on inherited thrombophilias: limited evidence guides screening; screening for MTHFR polymorphisms or fasting homocysteine is not recommended in pregnancy evaluation.

references.authors: Crider KS, Zhu JH, Hao L, et al.
references.title: MTHFR 677C->T genotype is associated with folate and homocysteine concentrations in a large, population-based, double-blind trial of folic acid supplementation.
references.finding: MTHFR TT women had lower folate and higher homocysteine at every folic acid dose, but genotype did not interact with dose: folic acid raised folate across all genotypes.

references.authors: Li F, Qi JJ, Li LX, et al.
references.title: MTHFR C677T、MTHFR A1298C、MTRR A66G and MTR A2756G polymorphisms and male infertility risk: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: MTHFR C677T was associated with male infertility and abnormal semen, mainly in Asian studies; A1298C was not.

references.authors: Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
references.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022.
references.finding: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline update: assess male lifestyle (strong); sperm DNA fragmentation testing can be considered for explanatory and diagnostic purposes (conditional); thrombophilia screening recommendations from 2017 were unchanged.

references.authors: Cappellini MD, Fiorelli G
references.title: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.
references.finding: G6PD deficiency, an X-linked defect affecting over 400 million people, causes neonatal jaundice and acute hemolysis triggered by oxidant drugs, infections or fava beans; management is avoidance of oxidative triggers.

references.authors: Luzzatto L, Ally M, Notaro R
references.title: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.
references.finding: About 500 million people carry G6PD mutations; most are asymptomatic but can develop severe acute hemolysis after fava beans, drugs such as primaquine or rasburicase, or infection.

references.authors: Gammal RS, Pirmohamed M, Somogyi AA, et al.
references.title: Expanded Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium Guideline for Medication Use in the Context of G6PD Genotype.
references.finding: CPIC classifies dapsone, methylene blue, pegloticase, primaquine, rasburicase, tafenoquine and toluidine blue as high-risk in G6PD deficiency, nitrofurantoin as medium risk, and vitamin C at standard doses as low-to-no risk.

references.authors: Nkhoma ET, Poole C, Vannappagari V, et al.
references.title: The global prevalence of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: G6PD deficiency affects an estimated 400 million people, with the highest prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa and malaria-endemic regions.

references.authors: Alangari A, Arif J, Al Qureshah F, et al.
references.title: Clinical benefits and risks of high-dose intravenous vitamin C: a systematic review.
references.finding: Systematic review of high-dose IV vitamin C: benefits in sepsis and cancer remain exploratory, and risks include oxalate nephropathy and hemolysis at very high doses in G6PD deficiency, supporting pre-infusion testing.

references.authors: Beretta A, Manuelli M, Cena H
references.title: Favism: Clinical Features at Different Ages.
references.finding: Favism (hemolysis after fava beans in G6PD deficiency) varies widely in severity, is most severe in young children and pregnancy, and often needs hospitalization and transfusion.

references.authors: Miyata M, Smith JD
references.title: Apolipoprotein E allele-specific antioxidant activity and effects on cytotoxicity by oxidative insults and beta-amyloid peptides.
references.finding: In cell culture apoE isoforms protected against hydrogen peroxide toxicity with E2 > E3 > E4, suggesting lower antioxidant activity of apoE4.

references.authors: Minihane AM, Jofre-Monseny L, Olano-Martin E, et al.
references.title: ApoE genotype, cardiovascular risk and responsiveness to dietary fat manipulation.
references.finding: APOE4 carriers may have 40-50% higher CVD risk, but associations are highly heterogeneous and diet-genotype interaction evidence comes from small or retrospectively genotyped studies.

references.authors: Keaney JF Jr, Larson MG, Vasan RS, et al.
references.title: Obesity and systemic oxidative stress: clinical correlates of oxidative stress in the Framingham Study.
references.finding: Urinary 8-epi-PGF2alpha was higher with female sex, smoking, diabetes and BMI, and lower with older age.

references.authors: Basu S, Helmersson J, Jarosinska D, et al.
references.title: Regulatory factors of basal F(2)-isoprostane formation: population, age, gender and smoking habits in humans.
references.n: 588 healthy adults in Sweden, Italy and Poland
references.finding: Urinary F2-isoprostanes differed by country, were higher in smokers, fell moderately with age, and were only slightly lower in women than men.

references.authors: Kander MC, Cui Y, Liu Z
references.title: Gender difference in oxidative stress: a new look at the mechanisms for cardiovascular diseases.
references.finding: Under physiological conditions women appear less susceptible to oxidative stress, possibly via estrogen and lower NADPH-oxidase activity, but hormone therapy did not reduce cardiovascular risk.

references.authors: Liguori I, Russo G, Curcio F, et al.
references.title: Oxidative stress, aging, and diseases.
references.finding: Review of oxidative stress as a contributor to ageing and age-related diseases; antioxidant therapy efficacy remains unproven.

references.authors: Block G, Dietrich M, Norkus EP, et al.
references.title: Factors associated with oxidative stress in human populations.
references.finding: Sex was the strongest predictor of lipid peroxidation (women higher F2-isoprostanes and MDA), stronger than smoking; plasma vitamin C was strongly inversely associated.

references.authors: Celis-Morales C, Livingstone KM, Marsaux CF, et al.
references.title: Effect of personalized nutrition on health-related behaviour change: evidence from the Food4Me European randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: Personalized nutrition advice improved diet more than generic advice, but adding phenotype or genotype (five diet-responsive variants) did not enhance its effect.

references.authors: ACMG Board of Directors
references.title: Direct-to-consumer genetic testing: a revised position statement of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics.
references.finding: ACMG position statement on direct-to-consumer genetic testing: consumers should be informed about test limitations, clinical validity and utility, and have access to a qualified genetics professional.

references.authors: King A, Graham CA, Glaister M, et al.
references.title: The efficacy of genotype-based dietary or physical activity advice in changing behavior to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, type II diabetes mellitus or obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Genotype-based dietary or physical-activity advice did not change behaviour more than general or phenotype-based advice.

references.authors: Camp KM, Trujillo E
references.title: Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: nutritional genomics.
references.finding: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: nutritional genomics is an emerging science; for complex chronic disease, genetic variants are only partially predictive and DTC testing is loosely regulated, so evidence-based validation is required before clinical use.
